newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians flock to vote in general election.
newsitem.headline: Romanians flock to vote in general election.

text.p: Romanians flocked to polling stations on Sunday to choose between President Ion Iliescu's moderate post-Communist reforms and the centrist opposition's pledge of swift action to tackle widespread poverty.
Iliescu, 66, one of 16 candidates for president, has been in office since taking charge of Romania in the aftermath of the 1989 revolution that ousted dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.

Despite jibes that he has done little to end communist-era decay, he holds a slight lead in opinion polls and will likely enter a run-off later this month against either professor Emil Constantinescu, 56, or former Prime Minister Petre Roman, 50.
"I will vote for Iliescu because I know him best," said Nela Mocanu, 31, one of only a handful of voters on Bucharest streets openly admitting their support for the president.
"Perhaps things are better elsewhere in eastern Europe but is that his fault? It's a matter of how people work."
Even if he does win, Iliescu could face a hostile parliament as his Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), tainted by corruption scandals, trails in parliamentary elections.

By 3 p.m. on a warm autumn day, 38 percent of voters had cast ballots. Romania's election commission predicted a "fine turnout" by the time polls were due to close at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT). They can remain open until midnight if needed.
A high turnout is thought to be in Iliescu's favour as his voters are generally less disciplined than those of Constantinescu's Democratic Convention (CDR).
Iliescu portrays his opponents as risk-takers and himself as a guarantor of stability able to avoid the more dramatic economic slide of Bulgaria and ethnic conflicts of Yugoslavia.

But many of the 17 million voters appear disgusted at soaring prices, charges of ruling party incompetence and an economic slump that has pushed living standards well below those of Hungary, Poland, and the Czech Republic.
"I want a better life for my family," said Grigore Vasile, 40, a rail worker in the resort of Sinaia, north of Bucharest. "I want new faces. Seven years with the same people is enough."
City voters, hardest hit by industrial decline, appear particularly distrustful of the president, who has come to rely on rural areas for his support.
"I regard these elections as a normalisation of the general climate and the general political development of our country," Iliescu told Reuters after after he and his wife Nina voted.
His comments were directed at Western suspicions of the democratic credentials of his administration and opposition allegations of mass attempts to rig the outcome.
Romania's campaign to join NATO and the European Union depends on a free and fair election. It is the only east European state where anti-communists have not been in power.
Constantinescu predicted victory after voting with his wife and two children in a district of drab apartment blocks.
Both Iliescu's main rivals push tax cuts, honest government and faster reforms and have formed a tactical alliance to guard against fraud. But they have made no post-election pacts.

Voters were handed booklets listing up to several dozen candidates and told to mark their choice with a stamp provided by officials. Hundreds of people failed to appear on electoral registers but were still able to vote on "special lists".

Several complaints of irregularities had been registered by late afternoon. The independent Mediafax news agency said one man in eastern Vaslui county committed suicide after being caught stealing ballot papers.
